title: Modern C++ essentials
description: Small practice deck for move semantics, smart pointers, lifetime, and compile-time features.

questions.prompt: After `std::string b = std::move(a);`, what is true about `a`?

options.text: a is guaranteed empty and safe to read as empty
a is in a valid but unspecified state; only assign/destroy are always safe without further checks
a is destroyed and must not be touched at all
a still holds "hello"; move copies by default

questions.explanation: Moved-from objects must be left valid; the standard does not require a specific value for std::string.

questions.prompt: What does the Rule of Zero recommend for many modern C++ types?

options.text: Always write destructor, copy, and move for every class
Prefer types that manage no raw resources so special members can be defaulted or omitted
Never use move constructors
Delete all special members and use only placement new

questions.explanation: Compose RAII members (string, vector, unique_ptr) and let the compiler generate special members.

questions.prompt: Which statements about std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr are correct?

options.text: unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership and is movable but not copyable
shared_ptr shares ownership via reference counting
Copying a unique_ptr duplicates the managed object automatically
make_shared can reduce allocations compared with shared_ptr(new T)

questions.explanation: unique_ptr is move-only; shared_ptr shares ownership; make_shared typically allocates control block and object together.

questions.prompt: What is the main lifetime risk with std::string_view?

options.text: string_view always extends the temporary's lifetime
string_view may dangle if it outlives the character sequence it views
string_view copies characters like std::string
string_view cannot bind to temporaries

questions.explanation: string_view is non-owning; binding to a temporary string leaves a dangling view after the full-expression.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are undefined behavior in C++?

options.text: Signed integer overflow
Using an object after its lifetime ended (e.g. dangling pointer)
Throwing an exception of a user-defined type
Data race on a non-atomic shared variable

questions.explanation: Signed overflow, use-after-lifetime, and data races are UB; throwing user types is fine.

questions.prompt: How does consteval differ from constexpr on a function?

options.text: consteval functions must produce a constant; they cannot be called at runtime
constexpr forbids compile-time evaluation
They are identical synonyms since C++20
consteval only applies to variables, not functions

questions.explanation: consteval means immediate function: every call must be a compile-time constant expression.

questions.prompt: Order these events for a block-scope object from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: Lifetime starts when initialization finishes and ends when the destructor starts.

questions.prompt: For a derived object, order construction from earliest to latest.

items.text: Non-static data member constructors (in declaration order)

questions.explanation: Bases, then members in declaration order, then the constructor body.

questions.prompt: Match each term to the best description.

right.text: Resource lifetime tied to object lifetime via ctor/dtor
Omitting copy/move of temporaries under permitted rules
Named return value optimization for a local returned by value

questions.explanation: RAII binds resources to objects; elision/NRVO avoid unnecessary copies of return values.

questions.prompt: Perfect forwarding typically uses std::{{fn}} on a forwarding reference T&&.
questions.explanation: std::forward preserves value category; std::move unconditionally casts to rvalue.

questions.prompt: To construct an element in-place in a std::vector, prefer v.{{method}}(...) over push_back of a temporary when it avoids an extra move.
questions.explanation: emplace_back forwards arguments to the element constructor in-place.

questions.prompt: In your own words: when should you apply the Rule of Five instead of the Rule of Zero?
questions.answerText: When your class directly manages a resource (raw pointer, socket, ownership not already handled by a member), you typically need a destructor and carefully defined copy/move operations (or =delete) — the Rule of Five. Prefer Rule of Zero by using RAII members so those special members stay defaulted.
questions.explanation: Self-check: resource-owning classes need explicit special members; otherwise compose standard RAII types.
